items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Driver of Managerial Competency Transformation: An Empirical Study of Telecommunications Operators in Tunisia
items.abstract: Résumé Objectif : Cet article examine comment l’intelligence artificielle (IA) transforme les compétences managériales dans le secteur tunisien des télécommunications, industrie fortement numérisée où les algorithmes soutiennent la segmentation de la clientèle, la maintenance prédictive et l’optimisation des réseaux. Les mécanismes par lesquels l’IA remodèle les compétences des managers demeurent peu explorés, en particulier dans les économies émergentes d’Afrique du Nord. Approche méthodologique : L’étude adopte une démarche quantitative, positiviste et hypothético-déductive. Mobilisant les théories des capacités dynamiques et des systèmes sociotechniques, complétées par les modèles d’acceptation technologique et la perspective institutionnelle, elle teste un modèle reliant l’IA, la confiance dans l’IA et la culture organisationnelle (variable modératrice) à quatre familles de compétences : collaboratives, augmentées, centrées sur l’humain et émergentes. L’IA est modélisée comme un construit réflexif de second ordre à six dimensions. Les données, recueillies par questionnaire auto-administré (échelles de Likert à sept points), sont analysées par PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4.0, 5 000 rééchantillonnages). Les hypothèses testent les effets directs des six dimensions de l’IA et les effets d’interaction de quatre dimensions culturelles (adoption, soutien organisationnel, intégration stratégique et formation). Échantillon questionné : 72 cadres supérieurs et top managers de Tunisie Télécom, Ooredoo et Orange (24 par opérateur), interrogés sur une période de quatre mois. Résultats : L’IA exerce un effet positif et significatif sur les compétences collaboratives (β = 0,53 ; p < 0,001) et augmentées (β = 0,41 ; p < 0,001). L’interaction homme-IA est le prédicteur le plus fort des compétences collaboratives (β = 0,71), et la confiance dans l’IA (β = 0,38) agit comme un mécanisme actif de développement des compétences. Les coefficients d’interaction, négatifs, suggèrent que la culture organisationnelle standardise l’influence de l’IA plutôt qu’elle ne l’amplifie. Originalité et implications : L’étude propose un modèle intégrateur IA–compétences–culture et une grille à quatre familles de compétences, et en tire des implications pour le recrutement, la formation continue, la construction de la confiance et la gouvernance de l’IA. Limites : Taille de l’échantillon et caractère transversal. Mots clés : intelligence artificielle ; compétences managériales ; transformation numérique ; PLS-SEM ; économies émergentes ; télécommunications ; Tunisie Abstract Purpose: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms managerial competencies in the Tunisian telecommunications sector, a highly digitalized industry in which algorithms support customer segmentation, predictive maintenance and network optimization. The mechanisms through which AI reshapes managers’ skills remain under-explored, particularly in North African emerging economies. Design/methodology/approach: The study adopts a quantitative, positivist and hypothetico-deductive approach. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems theories, complemented by technology acceptance models and an institutional perspective, it tests a model linking AI, trust in AI and organizational culture (moderator) to four families of competencies: collaborative, augmented, human-centric and emerging. AI is modeled as a second-order reflective construct with six dimensions. Data were collected through a self-administered questionnaire (seven-point Likert scales) and analyzed with PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4.0, 5,000 bootstrap resamples). The hypotheses test the direct effects of the six AI dimensions and the interaction effects of four cultural dimensions (adoption, organizational support, strategic integration and training). Sample: 72 senior managers and top executives of Tunisie Télécom, Ooredoo and Orange (24 per operator), surveyed over four months. Findings: AI has a positive and significant effect on collaborative (β = 0.53; p < 0.001) and augmented competencies (β = 0.41; p < 0.001). Human–AI interaction is the strongest predictor of collaborative competencies (β = 0.71), and trust in AI (β = 0.38) acts as an active mechanism of competency development. The negative interaction coefficients suggest that organizational culture standardizes the influence of AI rather than amplifying it. Originality and implications: The study proposes an integrative AI–competencies–culture model and a four-family competency framework, and derives implications for recruitment, continuous training, trust building and AI governance. Limitations: Sample size and cross-sectional design. Keywords: artificial intelligence; managerial competencies; digital transformation; PLS-SEM; emerging economies; telecommunications; Tunisia

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Dental Traumatology: A Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic, Predictive, and Decision-Support Performance
items.abstract: Introduction and aims Although artificial intelligence (AI) may improve early Traumatic dental injury (TDI) management, evidence across imaging diagnosis, risk prediction, large language model (LLM)-based decision support, and patient education remains unsynthesised. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, with PRISMA-AI principles consulted, we searched eight databases through 14 March 2026 for original studies evaluating AI in dental trauma. Methodological quality was appraised with design-specific tools (QUADAS-2, QUADAS-AI, PROBAST+AI, JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists, and RoB 2), supplemented by a structured AI-specific framework for LLM and chatbot evaluations. Reconstructable binary correctness data from non-clinical LLM, chatbot, or AI-assisted workflow studies were pooled using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with exploratory subgroup, sensitivity, and leave-one-out analyses, while remaining studies were synthesised descriptively. Results Thirty-seven studies spanning six evidence domains were included. Across 11 non-clinical LLM/chatbot evaluations, pooled accuracy was 0.798 (95% CI: 0.665-0.887), with extreme heterogeneity (I² = 99.66%) and a wide 95% PI (0.415-0.956), reflecting variability in systems, prompting strategies, and evaluation methods rather than a clinical performance benchmark. Disease-specific or workflow-enhanced systems (3 studies) showed numerically higher accuracy than general-purpose LLMs (8 studies; 0.957 versus 0.755), but the difference was not statistically supported (meta-regression P = .150), nor were other moderators. Imaging deep learning models (4 studies), predictive pipelines (4 studies), and one prospective clinical-validation study reported high task-specific performance (accuracy up to 0.919, mean average precision up to 0.995, and diagnostic accuracy up to 0.949). Overall, 11 studies were at high risk of bias and 25 at moderate risk. Conclusion Guideline-grounded tools show promise for time-critical TDIs; however, predominantly non-clinical, highly heterogeneous and moderate-to-high-risk evidence does not support readiness for clinical triage. Prospective, version-locked, independently and externally validated real-world clinical studies with transparent AI-specific reporting are needed before AI systems are recommended for clinical triage or emergency dental decision-making. Clinical relevance AI showed promising but highly variable accuracy in dental trauma (pooled 0.798 across 11 non-clinical studies; 95% PI: 0.415-0.956). Guideline-anchored and disease-specific systems performed numerically better than general-purpose LLMs, although this indirect difference was not statistically confirmed. These tools may support non-specialists in time-critical TDIs but require independent external validation and prospective real-world assessment before being recommended for clinical triage.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Challenges and Managerial Risks
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become a near-universal part of students’ academic practice, confronting universities with challenges that reach beyond technology to the core of teaching and assessment. This article is an integrative narrative review of peer-reviewed studies, preprints and policy documents published mainly between 2023 and 2026. It examines the crisis in the validity of knowledge assessment and the unreliability of AI detectors; cognitive dependence, metacognitive laziness and the erosion of critical thinking; digital inequality; the meta-analytic evidence on learning effects; and the regulatory framework set by UNESCO, the OECD and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The cross-cutting theme is the “performance–learning gap”: GenAI reliably improves task performance, but genuine learning gains depend on teacher support, pedagogical guardrails and the way students use the tool, and they often disappear when knowledge is assessed without AI. Particular attention is given to Georgia, where AI uptake is already high while the institutional response remains fragmented. The article proposes structural reform of assessment, a five-stage institutional pilot model for Georgian universities, a practical formula for students (“think first, ask AI, then evaluate critically”) and a research agenda of six priority directions.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HIGHER EDUCATION: OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES, AND THE WAY FORWARD
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly redefining higher education by transforming teaching-learning processes, research practices, and institutional administration.AI-driven tools such as adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and automated assessment offer significant opportunities to enhance personalization, improve academic outcomes, and expand equitable access to quality education.In the Indian context, the integration of AI in higher education assumes greater importance under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasizes technology-enabled learning, multidisciplinary education, faculty capacity building, and inclusive growth.However, the adoption of AI also presents challenges, including infrastructural disparities, limited faculty preparedness, data privacy concerns, ethical issues, and algorithmic bias.This article examines the opportunities and challenges associated with AI in higher education, highlights the role of NEP 2020 in shaping AI-driven reforms, and discusses select Indian case studies to illustrate current practices.

items.title: Artificial intelligence large language models and the threat to human health – A consensus statement by AAIO
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients, clinicians, and health organizations to obtain, summarize, and generate medical information. Although these tools can improve access to information and reduce communication barriers, their fluent output can obscure important limitations. This narrative review examines how LLMs may harm human health through interacting technical, cognitive, clinical, and societal mechanisms. Risks include fabricated or incomplete information, contextually inappropriate advice, failure to identify emergencies, unsafe medication or procedural guidance, sycophantic responses to leading questions, and excessive user reliance. Vulnerable people seeking mental health support may be particularly susceptible to validating or dependency-promoting interactions. Beyond individual encounters, LLMs can amplify health misinformation, contaminate evidence-retrieval systems, reproduce inequities, expose sensitive health data, and undermine scientific integrity. Case reports and recent litigation illustrate potential severity but do not establish the incidence of harm or prove causation. Risk reduction requires complementary action by patients, clinicians, developers, health systems, and regulators. LLMs should be treated as fallible communication tools rather than autonomous clinicians: High-stakes outputs require independent verification, identifiable data require appropriate protection, and urgent symptoms require conventional emergency assessment. Evaluation using realistic patient conversations, sustained human oversight, and transparent post-deployment monitoring is essential if the benefits of medical LLMs are to be realized without avoidable harm. Real-world cases have been included to provide greater clarity on the gravity of the situation and the finer points of jurisprudence under consideration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Learning and Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills among Senior High School Students
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence-assisted learning and mathematical problem-solving skills among Grade 12 students at Sulu National High School, Sulu, Philippines. Anchored in instructional scaffolding and self-regulated learning principles, the study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional, descriptive-correlational research design using a structured questionnaire and mathematical problem-solving assessment. An illustrative dataset comprising 350 student records was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, analysis of variance, and multiple linear regression. The analysis yielded an overall mean of 3.37 for AI-assisted learning and an average mathematical performance score of 70.04%. Problem comprehension obtained the highest performance score (76.96%), while verification and interpretation recorded the lowest (63.18%). A statistically significant moderate positive relationship was identified between AI-assisted learning and mathematical problem-solving performance (r = 0.386, p < .001). Regression analysis indicated that AI-assisted learning dimensions explained 15.72% of the variance in mathematical performance, with accessibility and utilization emerging as a significant predictor. The findings suggested that AI-assisted learning could support mathematical understanding and problem-solving, although independent verification and critical evaluation remained important areas for improvement. The study recommended integrating AI-supported instruction with independent mathematical assessments, teacher guidance, and responsible technology utilization. Its educational implications aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) and Sustainable Development Goal 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) by promoting inclusive learning opportunities and responsible educational innovation. The proposed approach could contribute to educational and institutional sustainability by informing mathematics instruction, digital learning policies, and the development of independent problem-solving competencies. Further empirical validation was necessary to establish the applicability of these findings to the target student population.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Professional Development and Digital Teaching Competence Among University Lecturers: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education is transforming teaching and learning practices and creating new opportunities for the professional development of university lecturers. AI-supported professional development has the potential to strengthen lecturers' digital teaching competence through personalized learning, intelligent feedback, adaptive instruction, and AI-assisted pedagogical practices. However, the nature, effectiveness, and implications of these interventions remain insufficiently synthesized. This systematic review examines the relationship between AI-supported professional development and digital teaching competence among university lecturers. The review adopts a systematic literature review approach guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Relevant empirical studies were identified through a structured literature search and assessed against predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria through searches of selected academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC and Google Scholar. AI-supported professional development was operationally defined as professional learning activities incorporating identifiable artificial intelligence capabilities, including generative AI applications, intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning technologies, conversational AI, and AI-powered feedback systems. Conventional digital technologies without identifiable AI functionality were distinguished from AI-supported interventions. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, with two reviewers independently conducting the assessments and resolving disagreements through discussion and consensus. The review synthesizes evidence on the ways AI-supported professional development can contribute to university lecturers' digital teaching competence, particularly in digital pedagogical knowledge, technology integration, instructional design, assessment practices, personalized learning, and reflective teaching. In conclusion, AI-supported professional development represents a potentially valuable approach to strengthening university lecturers' digital teaching competence. items.title: Axiological Problems of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Between Technological Efficiency and the Humanization of Learning
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education offers opportunities to improve efficiency, personalize learning, and support educational activities. However, these benefits raise an axiological question concerning the extent to which technological efficiency contributes to meaningful learning and human development. This article examines the axiological problems associated with the use of AI in education, particularly the tension between technological efficiency and the humanization of learning. Using a literature review approach, this study synthesizes scholarly literature to examine educational values, pedagogical implications, and ethical considerations in AI integration. Through thematic comparison, the synthesis identifies recurring issues and conceptual relationships among the instrumental benefits of AI, student agency, pedagogical relationships, and ethical responsibilities in its use. These relationships are integrated into a conceptual framework comprising four interconnected dimensions: instrumental value, student agency, pedagogical relationships, and ethical-contextual responsibility. The framework emphasizes that the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by efficiency or the automation of learning activities, but should be assessed in terms of students’ independent thinking, the quality of pedagogical interactions, and ethical principles and contextual needs. This study offers an axiological perspective that connects these four dimensions to evaluate AI adoption in education, positioning technological efficiency as one consideration rather than the sole criterion of educational value. Since the proposed framework is developed through a conceptual synthesis of literature, further research is needed to examine its applicability across different educational contexts.

items.title: Beyond Availability: Understanding Employee Underutilization of Employer-Sponsored Employee Assistance Programs for Mental Health Care - An Integrative Theoretical Review and Recommendations
items.abstract: Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs) have become one of the most widely implemented organizational interventions designed to promote employee mental health and well-being. Over the past five decades, EAPs have evolved from occupational alcoholism programs into comprehensive behavioral health resources. Despite extensive employer investment and substantial evidence demonstrating favorable clinical and organizational outcomes, employee utilization rates remain consistently low relative to the prevalence of psychological distress within the workforce. This discrepancy presents an important theoretical and practical question: Why do employees frequently decline employer-sponsored mental health services that are confidential, readily accessible, and provided at little or no personal cost? This integrative review synthesizes research from organizational behavior, occupational health psychology, counseling psychology, human resource management, and health psychology to develop a comprehensive explanation for employee underutilization of EAP services. Rather than attributing low utilization to a lack of awareness or accessibility alone, the review argues that employees engage in a multidimensional decision-making process in which perceived organizational, interpersonal, and professional risks frequently outweigh anticipated psychological benefits. The review integrates evidence from six complementary theoretical perspectives—the Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behavior, Self-Stigma Theory, Organizational Trust Theory, Psychological Safety Theory, and Social Exchange Theory—to explain how individual beliefs and organizational conditions jointly influence help-seeking behavior. The paper concludes by proposing an integrated conceptual framework in which leadership behavior, organizational culture, confidentiality perceptions, workplace norms, and employee trust interact with individual cognitive appraisals to determine EAP utilization. Implications for organizational leaders, human resource professionals, and future research are discussed.

items.title: Beyond Placement Duration: Workplace Affordances, Constraints and Student Agency in a Work-Based Learning Programme
items.abstract: A twelve-month industry placement gives undergraduates time to encounter authentic work, but duration alone cannot ensure meaningful learning. This study examines the workplace conditions that support or constrain learning among students in a Malaysian liberal education degree with multidisciplinary study pathways and a structured twelve-month work-based learning (WBL) component. Thirteen students from one programme described specific workplace episodes in individual interviews informed by behavioural event interviewing; accounts were examined through reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes were developed: (1) access to meaningful work is distributed rather than guaranteed; (2) everyday problems become learning opportunities through repair and guidance; (3) learning is mediated by relationships and organisational rules; (4) organisational pressures can reduce opportunities to learn; and (5) students negotiate ways to learn within workplace constraints. Students reported that trusted assignments created opportunities to practise judgement and understand the consequences of their actions. Supportive feedback helped them learn from errors, whereas exclusion from information, changing supervisors and heavy workloads restricted participation. Hierarchy and limited voice also emerged in their accounts, although workplace culture were not measured. These single-programme, student-reported experiences were not corroborated by supervisors and do not support sector-wide generalisation. This exploratory study proposes development of mid-placement task and feedback audit for joint academic-industry review. Overall, quality in long-duration WBL depends on meaningful task access, responsive guidance and appropriate discretion, rather than time spent in industry alone.

items.title: Beyond Technological Acceptance: Understanding the Influence of AI-Induced Job Insecurity, Career Adaptability, and Organisational Support on Employee Readiness for AI-Driven HR Transformation
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into human resource management is transforming recruitment, employee development, performance evaluation, workforce planning and employee engagement. Although technological acceptance has received considerable research attention, employee readiness for AI-driven HR transformation cannot be explained solely through perceived usefulness, ease of use or intention to use technology. Employees may simultaneously recognise the potential benefits of AI and experience concerns regarding job displacement, skill obsolescence, professional identity and future career opportunities. This study develops and examines an integrated framework explaining employee readiness for AI-driven HR transformation through three interrelated dimensions: AI-induced job insecurity, career adaptability and perceived organisational support. Drawing on Conservation of Resources Theory, Career Construction Theory and the Job Demands–Resources perspective, the study proposes that AI-induced job insecurity negatively influences employee readiness, whereas career adaptability and perceived organisational support positively influence readiness. It further proposes that career adaptability and perceived organisational support moderate the negative relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and employee readiness. For demonstrating the proposed analytical approach, an illustrative quantitative dataset of 400 Indian IT employees is constructed. The hypothetical analysis indicates a negative association between AI-induced job insecurity and employee readiness, while career adaptability and perceived organisational support demonstrate positive associations. The illustrative moderation results also suggest that career adaptability and organisational support may reduce the adverse relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and readiness. These numerical findings are simulated and should not be interpreted as actual field evidence. The paper contributes a resource-oriented explanation of employee readiness that moves beyond conventional technology acceptance and offers a framework for future empirical investigation in India's technology-intensive employment environment.

items.title: Beyond Traditional Teaching: Exploring Teachers’ Perceptions and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
items.abstract: This study investigated teachers’ beliefs, attitudes, awareness, and perceived challenges regarding the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and learning at higher education institutions in Multan District, Pakistan. A descriptive quantitative survey design was employed. Data were collected through an online, self-structured questionnaire comprising 45 statements organized into three domains: awareness of AI tools, perceived impact on teaching effectiveness, student engagement and assessment, and challenges associated with AI use. Although the thesis reports that 290 faculty members were selected, 163 completed questionnaires (67 male and 96 female) were included in the reported analysis. Frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations were used for descriptive analysis, while independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA were used to examine group differences. Overall, respondents expressed favorable perceptions of AI and its potential contribution to routine academic tasks, lesson preparation, personalized learning, instructional methods, assessment design, and feedback. Lack of training, insufficient technological infrastructure, limited institutional support, ethical concerns, data privacy, and academic dishonesty were identified as important barriers. Department-based differences were statistically significant across all three perception domains. Gender differences were significant for awareness and perceived impact but not for challenges; no significant differences were reported by teaching sector, teaching experience, academic qualification, or academic position. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires teacher development, institutional support, adequate infrastructure, and clear ethical and academic policies. As the data represent teachers’ perceptions, the findings should not be interpreted as direct evidence of improved student achievement.

items.title: Bloom’s Taxonomy in the Age of Generative AI: From Creation To Responsible Judgement Through Verify, Orchestrate, and Reflect (VOR)
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is challenging established assumptions about the relationship between student-produced artefacts and evidence of cognitive achievement. This perspective paper argues that these developments do not render Bloom's Taxonomy dated, but require its reinterpretation for learning environments in which cognitive work can be distributed between learners and AI systems. The perspective retains Bloom's six cognitive processes of Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, and Create while reconsidering how each is demonstrated when AI can retrieve information, generate content, analyse problems, and contribute to creative production. AI literacy is positioned as an enabling capability that operates across all levels rather than as an additional cognitive category. The paper further proposes Verify, Orchestrate, and Reflect (VOR) as three cross-cutting capabilities for AI-mediated learning. Verify concerns epistemic judgement and the ability to establish the credibility and evidential basis of information; Orchestrate concerns the strategic allocation, coordination, and supervision of cognitive work across human and AI resources; and Reflect concerns the ability to examine, explain, and take ownership of the reasoning and decisions underpinning an outcome. Their integration supports responsible judgement, conceptualised not as a seventh level of Bloom's hierarchy but as an emergent quality of higher-order performance. The paper therefore proposes a shift from production-centred evidence of learning to judgement-centred evidence, arguing that creation remains important but its educational value increasingly depends on the quality of human judgement surrounding it. The paper develops implications for assessment through oral defence, authentic tasks, process documentation, AI critique, and verification-focused activities. The proposed framework provides a basis for curriculum and assessment design that preserves Bloom's enduring emphasis on cognitive complexity while responding to the epistemic, strategic, and reflective demands of human-AI learning environments.

items.title: Bounded AI Assistance in Higher Education: Re-Aligning Pedagogy, Assessment and Institutional Governance
items.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has led universities and other higher education institutions to rethink the ways in which knowledge is conveyed, learning is facilitated, and academic performance is evaluated. While such technologies present possibilities for tailored explanations, feedback that supports learning as it unfolds, and joint inquiry, they also give rise to concerns regarding inaccurate information, reliance on machines for thinking, academic integrity, and inequities in access. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of selected literature and institutional guidance, this conceptual paper explores the pedagogical ramifications of LLMs. The paper contends that integrating them effectively demands learning and research environments that bring together subject-specific knowledge, critical questioning, openness about bounded AI use, and demonstrable competence. Constructive alignment, self-regulated learning, cognitive load theory, and cognitive engagement supply the conceptual bases for linking intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment. A cyclical process is put forward, comprising independent engagement, AI-assisted interaction under guidance, verification, application, and reflection. The paper goes on to elaborate dimensions of institutional policy, encompassing governance, curriculum, assessment, research integrity, privacy, intellectual property, equity, procurement, and quality assurance. Specific consideration is devoted to contexts with constrained ICT resources. The paper's conclusion is that the educational value of LLMs rests on purposeful design of specific institutional AI policy that is clear, transparent and progressive.

items.title: Capability atrophy: When AI automation erodes the dynamic capabilities it was meant to build
items.abstract: Firms adopt artificial intelligence (AI) automation to strengthen their dynamic capabilities, yet automation can also remove managers from the routines through which those capabilities are renewed. Drawing on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, organizational learning theory, and the automation–augmentation paradox, this conceptual paper develops the concept of capability atrophy and specifies when AI automation weakens, rather than builds, firm-level dynamic capabilities. Theory synthesis across research on skill erosion, organizational learning, and human–AI collaboration yields nine propositions, together with a multilevel, multi-wave mixed-methods design that uses behavioral and system-discontinuance measures to test them. The propositions hold that automation intensity relates to dynamic capability change in an inverted-U pattern, turning negative beyond a substitution threshold. Erosion travels through reduced experiential engagement, weaker skill retention, and poorer reliance calibration, and it becomes organizational when tacit knowledge is concentrated and apprenticeship paths close. Retained decision roles, frequent exceptions, and task variety are proposed to raise the threshold, whereas analytics capability alone is not. The paper places capability atrophy within existing skill-erosion research and adds a firm-level, conditional account with explicit falsification criteria. For practice, it implies that managers should track override rates, unaided diagnosis time, and other observable indicators of capability retention alongside the returns on AI investment.

items.title: Challenges of Certifying Machine Learning Trustworthiness in High-Consequence Domains
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems increasingly operate in high-consequence applications where trustworthiness assessment is critical, yet stakeholders often lack the information necessary to appropriately calibrate their trust in these systems. We argue that the challenge of assessing ML trustworthiness is fundamentally one of information asymmetries that exist between developers and stakeholders, and between complex models and all human actors, including their creators. These information gaps systematically impair trust development, leading to either over-trust or under-trust in ML systems. This paper advances three claims: first, that information asymmetries fundamentally impair appropriate trust development in ML systems; second, that systematic assessment and certification processes can reduce these asymmetries by creating standardized vocabularies and evaluation procedures; and third, that organizational maturity practices directly enhance trustworthiness rather than merely signaling it. We survey existing approaches to ML trustworthiness, identify critical obstacles to effective certification, and analyze methods for reducing information asymmetries through techniques such as intelligibility and provenance metadata.

items.title: Coaching and Inclusive Lifelong Learning within an AI-Supported Skilling System
items.abstract: This paper first explains how skilling systems improve workers' and firms' capacity to adapt to changing labour markets by helping them develop adequate skills, measure progress, and reward practice in distinct tasks. Coaching within skilling systems supports managers and employees in improving performance, managing workplace challenges and transitions, pursuing life goals, and developing leadership skills. Lifelong learning helps employees and employers remain successful within their own job and generally in the labour market. Inclusive lifelong learning within a skilling ecosystem ensures that continuous education, upskilling, and reskilling opportunities reach all people regardless of background, age, or employment status. AI-supported skilling systems, like those described in this paper, use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve coaching and lifelong learning by delivering personalized coaching and removing traditional barriers to education. This also helps to identify skill gaps and adapt educational content. Multilingual translations and real-time language conversions using AI make training more inclusive and available to marginalized groups and those with basic skill gaps. AI-based chatbots and mentors support "learning in the flow of work," continuous coaching and mentoring. AI can identify industry trends, and upskilling or reskilling programs can align with existing needs. Inclusive skilling ecosystems, which are also described in the paper, use artificial intelligence to support learning, job training, and career growth fairly and are open to all people.

items.title: Compensatory Resilience and Crisis Management: When Informal Practices Substitute for Formal Systems. A Qualitative Study of Tunisian Organizations (2011–2025)
items.abstract: RésuméObjectif. Cet article identifie et hiérarchise les facteurs de résilience organisationnelle mobilisés par des organisations tunisiennes durant la décennie de crises 2011-2025 (révolution, crises sécuritaires, pandémie de COVID-19, tensions sociales, technologiques et environnementales), et analyse l’articulation entre dispositifs formels et pratiques informelles. Problématique. La littérature conçoit la résilience comme une capacité d’anticipation, de réaction et d’adaptation, mais elle documente surtout des organisations dotées de dispositifs formels de gestion de crise stabilisés ; on sait moins ce qui fonde la résilience lorsque ces dispositifs sont lacunaires, centralisés ou privés de ressources, dans un contexte d’instabilité institutionnelle durable. Cadre théorique. Nous mobilisons quatre cadres complémentaires : la résilience comme capacité, la construction collective du sens, les pratiques réelles et le bricolage, et l’apprentissage organisationnel. Approche méthodologique. Dans une posture interprétativiste et un raisonnement abductif, nous menons une enquête qualitative exploratoire par entretiens semi-directifs, analysés sous NVivo 20 par une analyse thématique hybride, déductive et inductive. Échantillon. Vingt responsables de la gestion de crise, choisis par échantillonnage raisonné à diversification maximale, ont été interrogés dans vingt organisations issues de dix secteurs d’activité (treize publiques ou parapubliques et sept privées). Résultats. Organisés selon les étapes de la gestion de crise (détecter, gouverner, piloter, apprendre), les résultats sont synthétisés en une classification de quatre catégories de facteurs (structurants, compensatoires, dynamiques, contextuels), traversées par deux facteurs transversaux : le facteur humain et la tension entre dispositifs formels et pratiques informelles. La résilience observée est largement compensatoire : les acteurs pallient les déficits des dispositifs formels par des ressources informelles (réseaux de terrain, confiance, improvisation collective, coopérations), qui sont à la fois la principale force et la principale fragilité des organisations, car elles dépendent des individus. Originalité et apports. L’étude propose une lecture compensatoire de la résilience, formule huit propositions destinées à être testées et met en évidence des régimes de crise chronique et une dimension symbolique de la résilience. Implications managériales. Dix pistes d’application sont proposées aux responsables de la gestion de crise. Limites. Le codage a été réalisé par un seul chercheur, les données sont déclaratives et les PME sont faiblement représentées.Mots clés : résilience organisationnelle ; gestion de crise ; pratiques informelles ; facteur humain ; apprentissage organisationnel ; TunisieAbstractPurpose. This article identifies and ranks the organizational resilience factors that Tunisian organizations drew on during the decade of crises from 2011 to 2025 (the revolution, security crises, the COVID-19 pandemic, and social, technological and environmental tensions), and examines how formal systems and informal practices interact. Research problem. The literature conceives of resilience as a capability to anticipate, respond and adapt, yet it mostly documents organizations with stabilized formal crisis-management systems; far less is known about what sustains resilience when such systems are incomplete, centralized or under-resourced, in a context of lasting institutional instability. Theoretical framework. We draw on four complementary perspectives: resilience as a capability, collective sensemaking, actual practices and bricolage, and organizational learning. Methodology. Adopting an interpretivist stance and abductive reasoning, we conduct an exploratory qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews, analyzed in NVivo 20 through a hybrid thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding. Sample. Twenty crisis managers, selected through purposive maximum-variation sampling, were interviewed in twenty organizations from ten sectors (thirteen public or semi-public and seven private). Findings. Organized along the stages of crisis management (detecting, governing, steering, learning), the findings are synthesized into a classification of four categories of factors (structural, compensatory, dynamic and contextual), cut across by two transversal factors: the human factor and the tension between formal systems and informal practices. The resilience observed is largely compensatory: actors offset the shortcomings of formal systems with informal resources (field networks, trust, collective improvisation, cooperation), which are at once the organizations’ main strength and their main weakness, since they depend on individuals. Originality and contribution. The study offers a compensatory view of resilience, puts forward eight propositions to be tested, and identifies chronic-crisis regimes and a symbolic dimension of resilience. Practical implications. Ten practical recommendations are offered to crisis managers. Limitations. Coding was carried out by a single researcher, the data are self-reported, and SMEs are poorly represented in the sample.Keywords: organizational resilience; crisis management; informal practices; human factor; organizational learning; Tunisia

items.title: CONTROLLING AUTONOMOUS AI AGENTS : A Comparative Survey of Runtime Enforcement, Agent Architecture, Multi-Agent Monitoring and Collective Behaviour Detection
items.abstract: The rapid development of autonomous artificial intelligence agents raises a fundamental architectural question: How can human authority be preserved when AI systems increasingly plan, select, execute and adapt their own operational activities? Research addressing this challenge is developing across several distinct areas: runtime authorization, least-privilege access control, execution isolation, formal policy verification, system observability, anomaly detection and multi-agent coordination monitoring. This survey examines representative initiatives in these areas, with particular attention to thedistinction between controlling individual agent actions and identifying collective behaviour emerging through interactions among multiple agents. Nine principal research initiatives are examined: Faramesh, Tether, AgentGuardian,MCP-Secure, IsolateGPT, ACE, SentinelAgent, LumiMAS and Parity Swarm. A separate published systematic review of 58 primary studies is also considered asbackground evidence concerning the distribution of runtime-enforcement research. The survey then examines the ST-T1024 A1–A16 architecture and its complementary A17proposal for detecting emergent collective behaviour. The objective is not to establish the superiority of one architecture. It is to identify existingcontributions, examine their respective boundaries, expose unresolved research questions and establish a basis for independent technical comparison and experimentation. items.title: Designing AI for Learning, Not Answers: Learner Perceptions of Pedagogically Designed AI Interaction
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools become increasingly associated with rapid answer generation and task completion, students may come to rely on them for their speed, convenience, and immediacy. These expectations can create tensions for pedagogically designed AI agents that are intended to support guided reasoning and reflective learning rather than provide direct answers. However, limited research has examined how students perceive pedagogically designed AI agents within an authentic higher education environment. This study examined students’ perceptions of pedagogically designed GenAI agents implemented in an undergraduate auditing module at a Singapore higher education institution. Using a pre- and post-intervention survey design involving 49 final-year students, the findings indicate that although students recognised the educational value of the agents, their evaluations remained shaped by efficiency-oriented expectations associated with general-purpose large language models (LLMs). This study contributes to discussions on pedagogical AI design by highlighting tensions between efficiency and productive struggle in AI-supported learning.

items.title: Desktop review of Australian surveillance coverage of active and micromobility users
items.abstract: Background Active and micromobility transport modes, including bike riding, e-bikes, e-scooters and walking, are growing in popularity across Australia. As mode share grows, understanding their road safety profile becomes crucial. However, the extent to which Australia’s existing data infrastructure supports such surveillance has not been systematically examined. Methods We conducted a structured desktop review of Australian data sources relevant to injury, crash and exposure surveillance of active and micromobility users. Google-based searches, informed by published frameworks were conducted in August 2025. Sources underwent data extraction to capture scope, geographic and temporal coverage, coding systems, and mode-specific coverage. Results Ninety-seven data sources were identified: 41 injury sources, 13 police-collected or government-collated crash sources, 11 sources containing both crash and injury data, and 32 exposure sources. No ambulance, emergency department, or primary care source could reliably identify injured active or micromobility users from structured data fields. Hospital and deaths data could systematically identify pedestrians and pedal cyclists. Only Queensland and Tasmania could identify e-scooters in police crash data, and no jurisdiction differentiated e-bikes from pedal bicycles. items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the clinical effectiveness and alert performance of artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support systems in medication-related healthcare. Seven studies were included, comprising four comparative clinical evaluations and three primarily alert-performance evaluations. The review examines medication-error reduction, clinical alert validity and clinician response using outcome-specific quantitative synthesis. The original literature screening, eligibility assessment and initial data extraction were undertaken by the lead investigator. The research team was subsequently expanded to five authors during manuscript preparation and verification. The project maintains a transparent record of its protocol, methodological decisions, evidence extraction, statistical analyses and subsequent amendments. The protocol was documented retrospectively and was not prospectively registered. Target journal: International Journal of Medical Informatics.

items.title: DTAL : THE DETERMINISTIC TRANSACTION AUTHORIZATION LAYER. Paper 1: The Necessity, Threat Environment and Operating Principles of Autonomous Transaction Authorization in Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: The rapid development of autonomous artificial intelligence agents introduces acybersecurity challenge that extends beyond the protection of conventional informationsystems. AI agents can independently plan tasks, invoke tools, communicate with external services, access data and initiate operations. When multiple agents interact, their combinedactivity may also produce collective behaviour that was not explicitly specified by theirindividual operating instructions. Traditional cybersecurity controls remain essential. However, an organisation deployingautonomous agents needs an additional architectural answer to a fundamental question: Who has the final authority to authorize an external transaction initiated by thecompany's AI ecosystem? This paper proposes the Deterministic Transaction Authorization Layer (DTAL) as theexclusive authorization authority for such interactions. DTAL is designed to integrate with the ST-T1024 deterministic AI architecture and its agentic extensions A0–A16. It also incorporates A17, a research proposal for detecting emergent collective behaviour in multi-agent systems. Under the proposed arrangement, the company's AI agents operate autonomously within defined boundaries. DTAL independently evaluates and authorizes or refuses consequential external transactions according to policies established by the company. Individual human approval is not required for routine transactions. Authorization must operate at machine speed. The architecture also proposes duplicated DTAL supervision for continuity, with the CEO and CFO holding the two human governance keys for exceptional changes to the authorization authority. This paper establishes the threat environment, rationale and operating principles. Thedetailed technical architecture, protocols, interfaces, security mechanisms and verification requirements are addressed in its companion paper : Paper 2: DTAL — Architecture, Components and Authorization Protocol Keywords: Agentic AI, deterministic AI, cybersecurity, transaction authorization, multi-agent systems, collective behaviour, ST-T1024, A17, DTAL, process supervision.

items.title: Explainable AI for Fair and Transparent Human Resource Decision- Making
items.abstract: Human resource (HR) decisions are currently supported by algorithmic processes for hiring, promotions, and retaining employees, the lack of transparency in these models raises concerns about fairness, accountability, and trust of employees towards the process. In this paper, we develop a two-channel explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model that combines the post hoc explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME with the inherently interpretable classifier for HR decisions. In our methodology, adversarial debiasing is used in the training process to prevent the influence of sensitive attributes on the model performance. For testing the effectiveness of the proposed XAI model, we conduct an experimental evaluation using IBM HR analytics dataset with three HR decision making tasks including promotion prediction, attrition prediction, and candidate selection task. As results, we show that our model achieves reductions in demographic parity disparity without compromising the explanation quality using local accuracy and stability measures. Comparing with baseline models in terms of fairness-utility trade-off consistently yields improvements.

items.title: Exploring Cognitive Synergy Framework on Computing Students Epistemic Agency in Robotics Education
items.abstract: Generative AI can support robotics programming, but students must still evaluate suggestions and justify design decisions. This study examined changes in grit-related learning dispositions and patterns of epistemic activity during instruction using the Cognitive Synergy Framework (CSF). In a mixed-methods study across six West African universities, we randomly allocated 410 undergraduates to CSF-supported or comparison instruction. A categorical-time mixed-effects model analysed 848 Grit in Robotics Programming scores from 351 students across Weeks 11, 13, and 15. Epistemic network analysis examined coded actions from 30 collaborative groups. The reported GRP condition-by-time interaction was significant, Wald χ 2 (2) = 15.02, p < .001. Relative to Week 11, estimated gains were 0.167 points greater under CSF at Week 13 (95% CI [0.059, 0.274]) and 0.213 points greater at Week 15 (95% CI [0.093, 0.333]). With a 0.20-point downward adjustment to imputed CSF scores at both follow-ups, the joint test yielded p = .103. Group-level network trajectories differed by condition (β = 0.09, 95% CI [0.03, 0.15], p = .004). Gains in independent epistemic agency remained untested. Future studies should match instructional support across conditions and assess individual reasoning, evaluative judgement, and knowledge construction on tasks completed without scaffolding.

items.title: From competency lists to situation awareness-based evaluation for safe remote navigation in autonomous shipping
items.abstract: Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are reshaping maritime work by relocating safety-critical navigation from ship bridges to Remote Operations Centres (ROCs). This review examines whether research on MASS and ROC operator skills and competencies provides a sufficient basis for assessing their application during remote navigation. A combined bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review identified peer-reviewed studies from Web of Science, Scopus, and Transport Research International Documentation (TRID), with 48 studies included in the qualitative synthesis. The bibliometric analysis shows a fragmented field in which safety and navigation are prominent, while human-element and situation-awareness themes remain less consolidated. The thematic synthesis identified five competency domains: safety-critical cognition, digital-technical and Human–Machine Interface (HMI)-related competencies, reconfigured maritime operational expertise, communication and teamwork in distributed operations, and meta-competencies and adaptive capacity. These domains were interpreted through Endsley’s three-level Situation Awareness (SA) framework to examine how competencies may support perception, comprehension, and projection before decision-making and task execution. Although studies identify many competencies required for ROC operators, they provide much less evidence on how those competencies should be evaluated during safety-critical ROC performance. Future research should examine competency–SA relationships through task- and simulator-based assessment before assuming direct transfer or inadequacy of existing maritime competencies.

items.title: From immersion to educational world-making: applying secondary world theory to AI-supported XR design in teacher education
items.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) research in education has focused on immersion, presence, engagement, simulation and experiential learning. These perspectives explain immersive learning but do not fully account for the quality of the worlds learners enter. A virtual environment may be visually compelling while remaining pedagogically shallow, weakly structured or ethically unexamined. This study develops and applies an educational adaptation of Secondary World theory to examine AI-supported XR design in teacher education. The study draws on a theory-driven secondary mixed-methods analysis of an intervention involving 140 pre-service teachers working in 24 teams. Participants designed 48 virtual environments across CoSpaces and Minecraft, using ChatGPT for scenarios, learner personas and critique, and Spline for three-dimensional assets. The analysis examined team-level design artefacts, peer feedback, coded records and reflections across seven dimensions: coherence, depth, actionability, consequence, sub-creation, transfer and reflexivity. Four levels of educational world-making were identified: scenic immersion, task-world construction, pedagogical world construction and reflexive Secondary World-making. Most designs remained scenic or task-oriented, while fewer formed coherent pedagogical worlds integrating learner roles, actions, feedback and transfer. CoSpaces tended to support structured sequencing, while Minecraft supported spatial extension and collaborative construction. These patterns reflected platform affordances and design sequence. Generative AI was most strongly associated with higher-level world-making when used to test assumptions, accessibility, learner agency and pedagogical coherence rather than generate content. The study contributes a framework for evaluating XR learning environments beyond immersion and argues that teacher education should prepare future teachers to design, evaluate and critique the educational worlds technology makes possible.

items.title: From Learner Agency to Comparable Opportunities
items.abstract: This conceptual paper traces the connection between Jean-Pol Martin’s Learning by Teaching (Lernen durch Lehren, LdL) and the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR). It takes Martin’s 1985 dissertation on information processing in foreign-language teaching and his 1994 habilitation on the anthropological foundations of the curriculum as historical starting points. The paper makes explicit the normative premise that connects learner agency to institutional justice. If everyone’s basic needs deserve equal consideration, institutions should provide comparable effective opportunities to meet them. Two hypothetical examples, a classroom in which pupils take turns teaching and a municipal consultation, illustrate how access, support and influence determine whether people can meaningfully participate. The supplementary file Der Organismus als Ausgangspunkt contains the German translation of the AI-generated reconstruction by Le Chat that prompted this paper. items.title: From Organisational Trust to AI Adoption: Examining the Role of Perceived Fairness, Transparency, and Employee Confidence in AI-Enabled Human Resource Management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming human resource management (HRM) through its applications in recruitment and selection, performance evaluation, employee engagement, learning and development, workforce planning, and talent management. Despite the operational benefits of AI-enabled HRM, employee acceptance remains influenced by concerns regarding algorithmic fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and the reliability of automated decisions. This study develops and examines a framework explaining how perceived fairness, transparency, and employee confidence contribute to organisational trust and how organisational trust subsequently influences employees’ intention to adopt AI-enabled HRM systems. The study is conceptually grounded in organisational trust theory, organisational justice theory, and technology acceptance perspectives. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is proposed, with an sample of 160 employees and HR professionals working in Indian organisations. A structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale is used as the proposed measurement instrument. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, construct validity assessment, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression are applied to demonstrate the analysis. The findings indicate that perceived fairness, transparency, and employee confidence positively contribute to organisational trust in AI-enabled HRM. Organisational trust also demonstrates a positive association with employees’ intention to adopt AI-enabled HRM systems. The findings suggest that successful AI adoption in HRM depends not only on technological capability but also on organisational credibility, transparent decision-making, perceived procedural justice, and employee confidence. The study offers implications for Indian organisations seeking to implement responsible, trustworthy, and employee-centred AI-enabled HR practices.

items.title: From Vibe Coding to Automation, Implementation and the Cascade of Uncertainty
items.abstract: AI-native development environments are changing how digital products can be created, removing the barrier of human technical effort required to translate defined requirements into functioning software. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), this creates opportunities to participate more directly in digital production without requiring input from service providers. An appointment-based business case developed in an AI-native environment serves as one practical stress test of the implications of service design using Vibe Coding. The analysis distinguishes technical capability from economic sustainability and considers how integrated cloud services, AI computation, credit-based consumption and opaque cost attribution can complicate accountability for users with limited technical expertise. It concludes that a service provider cannot responsibly assume open-ended accountability for a system when its operating costs, dependencies and technical conditions may change beyond the provider's control. Connecting this use case to the industry's shift from Vibe Coding towards causal reasoning models and autonomous AI agents, this exploratory paper proposes quantum computing for the classification and optimisation of factory ontology data and in support of classical machine learning models. For critical manufacturing at scale, where token-based costs, energy use and sustainability goals may require it, quantum computing may provide the relevant evidence to inform and develop better tools that can intelligently manage the reliance of input by autonomous agents and black-box LLMs with that of lower expense deterministic, traditional algorithm-based logic.

items.title: Gamified Formative Assessment and Student Engagement: Measuring Cognitive and Affective Outcomes in STEM Classrooms. An Experimental Study in Imo State, South-East Nigeria
items.abstract: Gamified formative assessment, which adds game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards to low-stakes quizzes, is widely promoted as a way of increasing engagement, yet controlled evidence from sub-Saharan African STEM classrooms is scarce. This study tested the effect of gamified formative assessment on cognitive and affective outcomes among Senior Secondary 2 students in Imo State, South-East Nigeria. A pretest–posttest, delayed-posttest quasi-experimental design with a control group was used. Twelve intact Mathematics and Physics classes from 12 schools were randomly assigned to gamified assessment on digital quiz platforms (n = 158) or to non-gamified paper quizzes with the same items and feedback (n = 154) for eight weeks. After controlling for pretest scores, the gamified group outperformed the control group on the posttest, F(1, 309) = 124.13, p < .001, η²p = .29, g = 1.26, and on a delayed retention test four weeks later, F(1, 309) = 59.80, p < .001, g = 0.88. The gamified group also reported higher behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement (g = 0.84 to 1.15) and intrinsic motivation (g = 0.84), and slightly lower test anxiety (g = −0.23). Gender did not moderate the effect. The findings suggest that gamified formative assessment can improve both achievement and engagement in resource-constrained STEM classrooms, although novelty effects and the short duration warrant caution. Keywords: Gamification; Formative Assessment; Student Engagement; Motivation; STEM Education; Nigeria

items.title: Generative AI collaboration and expatriate career adaptability: a career construction perspective on sustainable career development
items.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) technologies become increasingly integrated into global workplaces, their implications for individual career development, particularly among internationally mobile professionals, remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and expatriates’ career adaptability, as well as three career sustainability-related outcomes: career satisfaction, life satisfaction, and perceived AI-enabled task performance. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, the study conceptualizes human–GenAI collaboration as a contextual resource associated with adaptive career responses. Drawing on data from 361 expatriates, the findings indicate that human–GenAI collaboration is positively associated with career adaptability, which in turn relates positively to these career-related outcomes. The results further show that the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and career adaptability varies according to expatriates’ AI trust and perceived AI-induced job insecurity. This study contributes to research on career development and human–AI interaction by highlighting the role of digitally mediated work practices in adaptive career processes within global work contexts.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence-related concerns among medical students in the West Bank, Palestine: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical education. However, concerns about its professional, ethical, and psychological implications for future physicians remain insufficiently studied, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study assessed GenAI-related concerns among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, using the Fear, Anxiety, Mistrust, and Ethics (FAME) scale. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling via online recruitment was conducted among medical students at Palestinian universities between March and April 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic and academic characteristics, prior GenAI tool use, self-reported level of AI concern, and FAME scores. Non-parametric tests and multiple linear regression were used for analysis. Results Of 399 participants included in the analysis, 96.0% reported using ChatGPT. The median total FAME score was 40 (IQR, 35–45). Median domain scores were highest for Mistrust and Ethics, both with a median score of 11, compared with Fear and Anxiety, both with a median score of 9. Male students had higher Fear and Anxiety scores than female students, but total FAME scores did not differ significantly by gender. In the exploratory adjusted regression model, no sociodemographic, academic, or AI-use variable was independently associated with the total FAME score, and the overall model explained only a small proportion of score variability. Conclusions GenAI use was widespread among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, with higher median scores observed in the mistrust and ethics domains than in fear of professional displacement. None of the variables included in the exploratory multivariable model was independently associated with total FAME score. Structured AI-literacy education addressing ethical reasoning and critical appraisal of AI-generated information may represent a potential educational implication of these findings.

items.title: Humanity on the Threshold of Flawlessness: Defending the Right to Err in an Age of Perfect Machines
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems have begun to produce faster and less error-prone results than humans in many domains, from education and health to science and governance. This opinion paper discusses an overlooked cost of this development: error is not merely a deficiency that humans should avoid, but a constitutive experience of learning, discovery, and meaning-making. The paper distinguishes three levels, termed functional perfection, human development, and existential meaning. It argues that technology can deliver major progress at the first level but cannot by itself resolve the other two. Findings from a recent study of a community of AI agents conducting science support this claim in two ways. On the one hand, even machines improve not by eliminating error but by making it visible and correcting it. On the other hand, agents that excel in experimental rigor lag behind humans in choosing significant questions and producing original contributions. After addressing possible objections, the paper proposes implications for education, research, and policy. Its central conclusion is that the education of the future should cultivate not individuals who answer better than AI, but individuals who can ask questions beyond AI’s answers, live with uncertainty, and preserve the right to learn through error.

items.title: Humanizing the Bot: How Conversational AI Responsiveness and Perceived Anthropomorphism Mitigate Customer Decision Hesitation Through Brand Trust
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots in e-commerce has restructured customer service delivery. However, online shoppers frequently experience pre-purchase decision hesitation due to transaction uncertainties. Grounded in Uncertainty Reduction Theory and Social Response Theory, this study investigates how Conversational AI Responsiveness and Perceived Anthropomorphism mitigate Customer Decision Hesitation through the mediating role of Brand Trust. Data were collected via an online survey from 195 e-commerce consumers in Indonesia who interacted with AI chatbots during their shopping journeys. The empirical framework was evaluated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. The empirical results reveal that both Conversational AI Responsiveness (β=0.482,p<0.001) and Perceived Anthropomorphism (β=0.325,p<0.001) significantly foster Brand Trust, while directly and indirectly mitigating Customer Decision Hesitation. Furthermore, Brand Trust operates as a vital complementary mediating mechanism (β=-0.395,p<0.001). The structural model explains 51.4 percent of the variance in Brand Trust and 48.7 percent in Customer Decision Hesitation. This research advances Marketing Technology literature by elucidating how humanized AI interactions alleviate choice anxiety, providing strategic guidelines for digital retailers to curb cart abandonment.

items.title: I Believe in You: Robot Identity Design and Service Initiative
items.abstract: Some public-service tasks involve requests for personal information, making a robot's presented role and service behavior relevant to users’ privacy perceptions. We examine professional identity cues and service proactivity in a simulated Chinese government-service setting. Semi-structured interviews ( \(n=17\) ) informed the study design; a pilot study ( \(n=34\) ) checked the manipulations; and a 2×2 within-subjects virtual study ( \(n=36\) ) measured self-reported privacy sensitivity and the depth of simulated disclosure. items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Students’ Academic Cost Reduction: A Comparative Analysis of Cost and Gender for Public Sector Universities in Hazara Division.
items.abstract: Despite the rapidly growing popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in universities, this study explores its impact on students’ academic costs at the higher education level. The study focuses on higher education students at public sector universities in the Hazara Division regarding the use of AI tools to minimise their educational costs. The study used quantitative data analysis and techniques in SPSS-26. It checked the reliability and validity of the data and then used regression analysis to meet the study objectives. Findings showed that effective utilisation of AI tools positively impacts students’ overall academic costs. Strategic integration of AI tools significantly contributes to lower academic costs, as shown in the gender-based analysis.

items.title: Impact of Perceived AI Threat on Unemployment Anxiety and Psychological Well-Being among IT Employees
items.abstract: This research seeks to analyze the connection between perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being of employees through a quantitative correlational approach. The emergence of artificial intelligence in the working environment raises worries in regard to job security and the threat of unemployment. Thus, there may be a rise in employment worries and a decrease in employees' mental well-being. The methodology to collect data on employees levels of perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being is based on surveying them using conventional self-reported questionnaires. Descriptive statistics will be used to analyze the levels of these factors in terms of their means (M) and standard deviations (SD). The reliability analysis is going to be done for checking internal reliability of a research tool using Cronbach's alpha. To measure the relationships between these three variables, a Pearson product-moment correlation will be used. Additionally, a simple linear regression will be run in order to see if perceived threat from AI can predict unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being and if unemployment anxiety can predict psychological well-being. The measurement of psychological well-being is going to be based on the six dimensions introduced by Ryff: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations with others, purpose in life, and self-acceptance. The results of this study will allow understanding how the way employees view AI being a threat to their jobs relates to worries about unemployment and psychological well-being. All in all, the results of this research can be helpful for realizing the significance of recognizing employees’ concerns in the course of technological changes and encourage businesses to provide adequate support to employees for mitigating job-related uncertainty and reaching psychological well-being.

items.title: INFLUENCE OF INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY (ICT) ON COGNITIVE ENGAGEMENT AMONG SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS IN MINNA METROPOLIS, NIGER STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study examined influence of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) on cognitive engagement among senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria. Two objectives guided the study, and two research questions were raised and answered. Two null hypotheses were formulated and tested at 0.05 levels of significance. Descriptive survey design was adopted for the study. The population of the study comprised of 3,023 senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State. The sample of the study was 311 senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State which was selected through multi-stage sampling procedure. Influence of Information and Communication Technology on Students’ Cognitive Engagement Questionnaire’ (IICTSCEQ) was used for data collection and it was validated by three experts from the Department of Counselling Psychology, IBBU Lapai. Test re-test method was used to obtain the reliability coefficient and co-efficient-value was 0.82. The data collected were analyzed through the use of Statistical Product for Service Solution (SPSS- version 24). Frequency counts and percentage were used to present the demographic information of the respondents, mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, simple linear regression was used to test hypotheses 1 and independent sample t-test was used to test hypotheses 2 at 0.05 levels of significance. The findings of the study revealed among others that ICT has a significant positive influence on cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis Niger State; and there is no significant difference between male and female respondents in the influence of ICT on cognitive engagement among senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis, Niger State. The study concluded that ICT significantly influences the cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students by improving critical thinking to learning. Based on these findings, the researcher recommended that Teachers should combine ICT tools with innovative teaching strategies that promote critical thinking and problem-solving skills to enhance the cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria; and School administrators and teachers should ensure that ICT instructional strategies are designed to equally stimulate the cognitive engagement of both male and female senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa y autorregulación del aprendizaje en la educación superior ecuatoriana: Una revisión sistemática
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to synthesize evidence regarding the relationship between the academic use of generative artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning among higher education students in Ecuador. A systematic literature review was conducted, involving a structured web-based search for publications in Spanish and English from the 2023–2026 period. Out of 25 identified records, five publications were selected. The selection process was documented using a diagram adapted from the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT 2018 instrument. The narrative synthesis revealed positive associations between the frequency of generative artificial intelligence use and both learning planning and monitoring. One intervention, which combined three artificial intelligence tools with pedagogical guidance, showed an increase in scores for goal setting and self-monitoring. Self-evaluation was addressed by only a single specific estimate, derived from a study that contained discrepancies in its reported sample size. It was concluded that, among the publications examined, the evidence was more consistent for planning and monitoring than for self-evaluation. Variations in research designs and instruments limited the ability to establish causal links or generalize the findings to the context of higher education in Ecuador.
